813.title: Mata Nanaki
813.hook: Guru Hargobind's wife, mother of Guru Tegh Bahadur, who kept faith through the Bakala years
813.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mata Nanaki as the wife of Guru Hargobind and the mother of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and tell the story of the Bakala years, when a crowd of claimants rose and the true Guru was found.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the week ended with Mian Mir, the Sufi friend who, tradition says, laid the Harmandir's foundation stone. Your line was friends across faiths. Did you honor someone whose path isn't yours? A new week begins with a woman who waited. Day eight hundred thirteen.

A promise with no date on it is a strange thing to live with. Someone you trust tells you: this will come. Not when. Not how. Just that it will. Then the years go by, and other things happen instead, and the people around you stop asking about it. Mata Nanaki lived with a promise like that, in a quiet town called Bakala, while the Guruship passed to others. Today: Mata Nanaki.
screen: `A PROMISE WITH NO DATE.` → `THE YEARS GO BY.` → `A QUIET TOWN CALLED BAKALA.`

segments.voice: Mata Nanaki was the wife of Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, and the mother of a quiet, inward son named Tegh Bahadur. When Guru Hargobind chose his successor, he didn't choose that son. He chose his grandson, Har Rai. Tradition says Guru Hargobind then asked Mata Nanaki to go to Bakala, with Tegh Bahadur and his wife, and told her something she held on to: in time, her son would sit in the Guru's seat. So she went. And she waited. Guru Har Rai became Guru, and served, and passed on. Then the child Guru, Har Krishan. All that time, tradition says, Tegh Bahadur lived quietly in Bakala, spending long hours in meditation, asking for nothing. His mother was beside him. Nothing in the story says she pushed, or campaigned, or complained that her son had been passed over. She kept faith that the promise would keep itself. Then, tradition says, Guru Har Krishan, as he was dying, named no one directly. He said only that the next Guru was at Bakala. And suddenly the quiet town filled up. Tradition says a crowd of claimants set themselves up there, each saying he was the one. The waiting was nearly over, and it got noisier, not easier. In the end, Sikhs say, a trader named Makhan Shah found the true Guru, Tegh Bahadur, and announced it from the rooftop. Mata Nanaki saw the promise kept. What she modeled wasn't passivity. It was a steady kind of trust: carrying on with an ordinary life, with prayer at its center, without forcing the thing she'd been told would come.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep faith while waiting. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Name one thing you're waiting on right now: news, a recovery, a change in someone, a door that hasn't opened. Hold it gently, like a letter you haven't opened yet. Notice the pull to force it, to check, to push. On each breath out, set the forcing down, and keep the hope. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. If not, just let the waiting be quiet for this sit. The bell holds the time.
Mata Nanaki. Guru Hargobind's wife and Guru Tegh Bahadur's mother, who waited at Bakala, tradition says, trusting her son would one day be Guru. Today's word.
Your line: she waited in faith. Today, when the thing you're waiting on comes to mind, leave it unforced one more time, and do one ordinary task well instead. Day eight hundred thirteen.

814.title: Bibi Viro
814.hook: Guru Hargobind's daughter, whose wedding went on amid battle
814.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bibi Viro's wedding as part of the story of Guru Hargobind's battle at Amritsar, and Sikh weddings, the Anand Karaj, are celebrated as a sacred part of householder life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Nanaki waited at Bakala, trusting a promise with no date on it. Your line was she waited in faith. Did you leave one thing unforced? Today, a daughter of the same household, and a date that wouldn't move. Day eight hundred fourteen.

The sweets were already made. The groom's family was on the road. The day had been fixed, and the whole household had been counting toward it. Then word came that soldiers were marching on Amritsar. It's a familiar shape: the celebration planned for months, and then the phone call, the diagnosis, the storm, the bad news that lands the same week. Do you call it off? Guru Hargobind's household faced that question with swords drawn. Today: Bibi Viro.
screen: `THE SWEETS WERE ALREADY MADE.` → `SOLDIERS MARCHING ON AMRITSAR.` → `DO YOU CALL IT OFF?`

segments.voice: Bibi Viro was the daughter of Guru Hargobind. Her wedding had been arranged and the day was set. Then trouble came. Tradition says it began with a quarrel between Sikhs and a royal hunting party over a hawk, and it ended with troops sent against the Guru at Amritsar, just as the wedding was close. Guru Hargobind had to fight. But he didn't cancel his daughter's wedding. Tradition says he sent the women and the bride away from the fighting, to a nearby village called Jhabal, and sent word to the groom's family to meet them there. The battle was fought at Amritsar. And at Jhabal, on the day that had been fixed, Bibi Viro was married. Tradition says the Guru himself came to give his daughter away once the fighting was over. Sit with the picture for a moment. Smoke over one town. Wedding songs in another, not far away. Both happening in the same family on the same day. The story doesn't pretend the danger wasn't real, and it doesn't pretend the wedding didn't matter. It holds them together. In Sikh teaching, a householder's life is not a lesser path than a life of withdrawal. Marriage, children, cooking, celebrating: these are part of the way, not distractions from it. In this story, a wedding isn't something given up the moment things get hard. It's one of the things worth protecting, and protecting it meant a new village, a message on the road to the groom's family, and a father arriving after the battle to give his daughter away.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a celebration going. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Then think of one good thing coming up, yours or someone else's, that the hard news around you might crowd out: a birthday, a small anniversary, a friend's good result, a meal you'd planned. See it clearly. Then decide, gently, that it will still happen, maybe smaller, maybe somewhere else, like the wedding moved to Jhabal. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bibi Viro. Guru Hargobind's daughter, married, tradition says, on the day fixed, while a battle was fought nearby. Today's word.

815.title: Mata Gujri
815.hook: wife of the ninth Guru, mother of the tenth, grandmother of the Sahibzade, steady to the end
815.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mata Gujri and the younger Sahibzade each winter, especially at Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib near Sirhind, with prayer, kirtan and the retelling of their story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bibi Viro was married at Jhabal while a battle was fought at Amritsar. Your line was joy amid trouble. Did you keep one celebration going? Today, a woman who was at Bakala too, and whose story ends in winter. Day eight hundred fifteen.

Near the town of Sirhind, in Punjab, there's a gurdwara called Fatehgarh Sahib, and close by stands a place Sikhs call the Thanda Burj, the cold tower. Some visitors stand there a long time, in no hurry. What they come for isn't the stonework. Others bring their children and grandchildren and tell them a story there, the same story that was told there once before, by a grandmother to her small grandsons on cold nights. Today: Mata Gujri.
screen: `FATEHGARH SAHIB, NEAR SIRHIND.` → `THE COLD TOWER.` → `A GRANDMOTHER AND HER GRANDSONS.`

segments.voice: Mata Gujri's life runs through three generations of the Guru's house. She was the wife of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and she was with him in the quiet years at Bakala. She was the mother of Guru Gobind Singh. And she was grandmother to the Sahibzade, the Guru's sons. She saw her husband leave for Delhi, where, Sikhs remember, he gave his life rather than let others be forced from their faith. She raised her son to lead. Then came the hardest winter. Tradition says that when the Guru's family left Anandpur under attack, they were scattered in the confusion of a flooded river crossing. Mata Gujri ended up alone with her youngest grandsons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh. A former servant of the household, Gangu, took them in, and then, tradition says, betrayed them to the authorities. They were taken to Sirhind and held in the cold tower. Tradition remembers what she did there. She didn't panic, and she didn't tell the boys to save themselves at any cost. She told them about their grandfather, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and the Gurus before him. She kept them steady. When the boys were brought before the governor, they refused to give up their faith, and they were put to death. Tradition says Mata Gujri died in the tower soon after. Sikhs also remember who spoke up. Tradition says the Nawab of Malerkotla, a Muslim noble, protested that children should not be punished this way. And a local man, Todar Mal, gave what he had so they could be cremated with honor. That's what steady to the end looks like here: not the absence of grief, but a grandmother who stayed herself, and kept her grandsons steady, until the very end.
screen: `WIFE, MOTHER, GRANDMOTHER.` · `SCATTERED AT THE RIVER.` · `SHE KEPT THE BOYS STEADY.` · `THOSE WHO SPOKE UP.` · then, large: `STEADY TO THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a grandmother. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind a grandmother: your own, someone else's, or an older woman who steadied you when you were young. See her hands, her voice, one thing she used to say. If she's living, think of one way to honor her this week: a call, a visit, a question about her life. If she's gone, simply thank her in your mind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mata Gujri. Wife of Guru Tegh Bahadur, mother of Guru Gobind Singh, grandmother of the Sahibzade, who kept her grandsons steady in the cold tower. Today's word.
Your line: steady to the end. Today, honor one grandmother, or an older woman who steadied you, by name: a call, a story told to someone younger, or a quiet thank you. Day eight hundred fifteen.

816.title: Kirpa Ram of Kashmir
816.hook: the pandit who led the plea to Guru Tegh Bahadur later joined the Khalsa and died at Chamkaur
816.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Kashmiri pandits' plea to Guru Tegh Bahadur each year on the Guru's martyrdom day, and Kirpa Ram's later life as Kirpa Singh is told as part of the story of Chamkaur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Gujri kept her grandsons steady in the cold tower. Your line was steady to the end. Did you honor a grandmother? Today, a man whose story is tied to her husband's. Day eight hundred sixteen.

A parent's years. A stranger who pulled you out of the water. A teacher who saw something in you nobody else did. None of those comes with a bill you can settle, or a sum you can hand back with interest. What you can do is spend the rest of your life near the person, or the cause, that saved you. That's the shape of today's story. It begins with a group of frightened men walking a long way from the mountains of Kashmir to Anandpur, to ask a Guru for help. Today: Kirpa Ram of Kashmir.
screen: `WHAT CAN'T BE PAID BACK.` → `FROM KASHMIR TO ANANDPUR.` → `ASKING A GURU FOR HELP.`

segments.voice: Kirpa Ram was a pandit, a Hindu Brahmin scholar, from Kashmir. Tradition says that in his time the Kashmiri pandits were being pressed by the authorities to give up their faith, and they didn't know where to turn. So Kirpa Ram led a group of them to Anandpur, to Guru Tegh Bahadur, and laid their plea before him. Sikhs tell what happened next with great reverence. Tradition says the Guru sat in silence, troubled, and said that a holy person would have to offer his life to stop this. His young son, Gobind Rai, the future Guru Gobind Singh, asked who could be worthier than his father. And Guru Tegh Bahadur, the story goes, told the pandits to send word: if the Guru can be made to change his faith, we will change ours too. He went to Delhi, and there he was executed. Sikhs remember him as one who gave his life for the freedom of others to keep a faith that wasn't his own. Then the story turns back to Kirpa Ram. He didn't go home and get on with his life. Tradition says he stayed close to the Guru's house, and taught the young Gobind Rai Sanskrit and the old texts. Years later, when Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, Kirpa Ram took amrit and became Kirpa Singh. And tradition says he was among those who fell at Chamkaur, in the same battle as the Guru's elder sons. The man who had come to ask for help came back, and stayed, and served, all the way to Chamkaur. He didn't pay the debt off. He lived inside it.

Bring to mind one person, or one community, that helped you at a moment when you couldn't help yourself. Let the memory be specific: where you were, what they did. Then notice the urge to settle the account and move on. Instead, ask: what would it look like to stay near this? A visit, a regular call, time given to the cause that once held you up. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Kirpa Ram. The pandit who brought the plea to Guru Tegh Bahadur and, tradition says, came back to serve, became Kirpa Singh, and fell at Chamkaur. Today's word.

817.title: Pir Budhu Shah
817.hook: a Sufi who sent his sons and followers to fight beside the Guru at Bhangani, where two sons fell
817.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Pir Budhu Shah in tellings of the battle of Bhangani and in talks and kirtan programs about the Muslims who stood with the Gurus, and his town of Sadhaura is remembered in that story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kirpa Ram of Kashmir, the pandit who once came asking for help and, tradition says, came back years later to serve. Your line was he came back to serve. Who keeps showing up for you? Today, a friend from another faith. Day eight hundred seventeen.

A recommendation can be a heavy thing to give. You put your name next to someone else's, and if they let the other person down, part of that is on you. Now raise the stakes. A holy man of one faith vouches for a band of soldiers to a teacher of another faith. The soldiers take the pay. Then, on the eve of a battle, most of them walk away. The holy man hears the news. He could send an apology. He could stay home. Instead, tradition says, he gathers his own sons and his own followers and rides toward the fighting. Today: Pir Budhu Shah.
screen: `HE VOUCHED FOR THEM.` → `THEY WALKED AWAY.` → `HE RODE IN HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Pir Budhu Shah was a Sufi, a Muslim teacher of the inner path, who lived at Sadhaura, not far from where the young Guru Gobind Singh was staying in the hills. Pir is a title for a spiritual guide. Tradition says the two men met and respected each other, and that the Pir recommended a company of Pathan soldiers who needed work. The Guru took them on. Then came Bhangani, the battle where hill rajas marched against him. Tradition says most of those Pathans deserted before the fighting, and only a few stayed. When the Pir heard what the men he had vouched for had done, he did not send excuses. He came himself, with his sons and his followers, to stand beside the Guru. And in that fighting, tradition says, two of his sons were killed. Hold that for a moment. A father of one faith lost two sons defending a teacher of another faith, because, the story says, his word had been given. After the battle, the story goes, the Guru wanted to honor him. Tradition says the Pir asked for the comb the Guru had just used, with strands of his hair still caught in it, and the Guru gave it to him, along with a turban. Some readers notice how small that request was: not land, not gold, just a comb. Sikhs remember Pir Budhu Shah with love. His story is told when people ask what friendship between faiths can look like. Not a polite handshake. Keeping your word when it costs you, beside someone who prays differently. And it reminds Sikhs that among the people around the Gurus were Muslims who gave everything.

If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.

818.title: Mata Jito
818.hook: Guru Gobind Singh's wife, whom tradition credits with the sugar in the first amrit
818.howItsDone: At an amrit ceremony, the Panj Pyare prepare amrit from water and patashas in an iron bowl, stirring it with a khanda while reciting set compositions, and Sikhs tell the story of the sweets being added by a wife of the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pir Budhu Shah, the Sufi who rode in with his sons when the soldiers he vouched for walked away. Your line was a sufi's sacrifice. Did someone from outside your circle come to mind? Day eight hundred eighteen.

An iron bowl. Clear water. A double-edged blade turning slowly through it, while hymns are recited over it, verse after verse. This is the scene Sikhs tell from the day the Khalsa was born at Anandpur: the Guru preparing amrit, the water of initiation. It's a scene of steel. And then, in the telling, someone steps forward with something small in her hands. Sugar. Little puffed sweets, dropped into the bowl. She doesn't make a speech. She just adds them. And the story says the Guru let them stay. Today: Mata Jito.
screen: `AN IRON BOWL, A DOUBLE-EDGED BLADE.` → `SOMEONE STEPS FORWARD.` → `SUGAR IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Mata Jito was a wife of Guru Gobind Singh. Mata means mother, a title of honor, and Sikhs use it for the women of the Guru's household. Tradition remembers her as the mother of several of the Guru's sons, the ones Sikhs call the Sahibzade. Now, the bowl. Amrit, the water of initiation, is made with water and sugar puffs called patashas, stirred with a khanda, a double-edged sword, while sacred compositions are recited. The sugar is part of it to this day. And the story Sikhs tell about how the sugar got there is a story about a woman. The Guru was stirring the steel through the water. A wife of the Guru came and added the sweets. One telling says the Guru took it as a sign: the Khalsa would be brave, and it would also be sweet. Here's where the sources differ, and it's worth saying plainly. Some tellings, including the one this path follows today, give the sweets to Mata Jito. Other tellings give the same moment to Mata Sahib Kaur, whom we meet in two days. Sikhs hold both tellings, and nobody needs to settle it to see the point. What is the point? Steel alone can make someone hard. A sword can protect, but it can also make a person proud, quick, cold. The story puts sweetness in the same bowl, so that whoever drinks it is meant to carry both: courage and gentleness, a straight back and a soft word. Sikhs speak of the ideal as saint and soldier together. This little story shows the saint half being stirred in, by a woman's hand, at the very bowl where the Khalsa began.
screen: `A WIFE OF GURU GOBIND SINGH.` · `WATER, STEEL AND SUGAR.` · `TWO TELLINGS, ONE MOMENT.` · `COURAGE AND GENTLENESS IN ONE BOWL.` · then, large: `SWEETNESS IN THE STEEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add sweetness to strength. Settle into the sit and let the breath slow. Think of one place in your life where you have to be strong right now. A hard conversation, a decision, a person you have to stand up to. Hold it lightly. Now ask: what would sweetness look like in that same moment? A kinder first sentence. A pause before answering. A thank-you you'd usually skip. Don't drop the strength. Just picture both in the same bowl. The bell holds the time.

819.title: Mata Sundari
819.hook: after Guru Gobind Singh, she guided the Sikhs through letters and counsel
819.tomorrow: Mata Sahib Kaur, mother of the Khalsa
819.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mata Sundari as a guide of the community after Guru Gobind Singh, and hukamnamas, letters of instruction, are still issued from the Akal Takht and read aloud to congregations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Jito, and the sweets dropped into the iron bowl beside the blade. Your line was sweetness in the steel. Did you manage to be firm and kind in the same breath? Day eight hundred nineteen.

A sheet of paper, folded and sealed. A rider carries it out of Delhi, along dusty roads, to a village where Sikhs are gathered and waiting for word. Someone opens it and reads it aloud to the whole room. It has blessings in it, and counsel, and requests, and it comes in the name of a woman. The Guru who led them in person is gone. The community is scattered and under pressure. And for a stretch of years, tradition says, a great deal of what held them together arrived like this: in letters, from a widow in Delhi. Today: Mata Sundari.
screen: `A SEALED LETTER LEAVES DELHI.` → `READ ALOUD TO THE SANGAT.` → `SIGNED BY A WOMAN.`

segments.voice: Mata Sundari was a wife of Guru Gobind Singh, and tradition remembers her as the mother of his son Ajit Singh, who fell at Chamkaur. When the Guru left Anandpur and the hard years came, she and Mata Sahib Kaur went to Delhi. Later the Guru traveled south, and he died there. Tradition says he named no person to follow him as Guru: the Guruship would rest in the scripture and in the Khalsa. So who would the Sikhs turn to with a question, a quarrel, a need? Tradition says they turned to Mata Sundari. The way she led was through hukamnamas. A hukamnama is a letter of instruction and blessing. The Gurus had sent them before her, to congregations far away. Now letters went out in her name, tradition says, to sangats across the Punjab and beyond: asking them to keep the Sikh way, to support the community's needs, to stay united, and blessing them. Sikhs remember her settling disputes and sending trusted Sikhs to care for holy places. Notice what kind of leading this was. No army. No throne. She didn't claim to be the Guru, and the tradition doesn't say she was. She led by being trusted, by writing, by counsel, by staying faithful to what the Guru had set up and asking others to stay faithful too. That fits this whole week. Mata Nanaki, who waited in faith. Bibi Viro, joy amid trouble. Mata Gujri, steady to the end. Kirpa Ram, who came back to serve. Pir Budhu Shah, a sufi's sacrifice. Mata Jito, sweetness in the steel. And now Mata Sundari, holding a scattered people together with ink and patience.
screen: `A WIFE OF GURU GOBIND SINGH.` · `NO PERSON AFTER HIM AS GURU.` · `LETTERS OF COUNSEL AND BLESSING.` · `LEADING BY BEING TRUSTED.` · then, large: `SHE LED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a letter of guidance. For the sit, just breathe and think. Who in your life could use a few lines from you right now? A younger cousin. A friend starting something new. A coworker who's struggling. Don't write it yet. Let the breath slow and ask what you'd actually want them to hear: one piece of counsel, one blessing, one thing you'd ask of them. Keep it short, the way a letter read aloud should be. After the bell, if it still feels right, write it down and send it. The bell holds the time.
Mata Sundari. A wife of Guru Gobind Singh who, after his death, guided the Sikhs from Delhi through letters and counsel. Today's word.

Your line: she led. Today, lead the way she did, with a few written words: one message of encouragement or advice to someone who's waiting to hear from you. Day eight hundred nineteen, and the end of a week.

screen: `DAY 819 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MATA SAHIB KAUR, MOTHER OF THE KHALSA.`
